paras: The Logansport manhunt was an armed pursuit in late July 1903 by farmers of Harrison township, near Logansport, Indiana, of an unidentified man accused of attacking Mrs. Joseph Watts near her home, which wire reports said would likely end in a lynching. After a chase with bloodhounds on July 28, the posse concluded that the man had escaped by train, and no capture was reported. Dispatches called the armed crowd a "posse" "intent on lynching," a usage the Baltimore Sun mocked and the Baltimore Afro-American put in quotation marks.

Mrs. Joseph Watts, wife of "a prominent farmer," lived in Harrison township about three miles from Lucerne, in Logansport's county. According to the Indianapolis Journal, she was walking home after dark on July 27 from the house of her son George Watts, half a mile away.

Several hundred feet from her home, the Journal said, a man who had been sitting under a tree beside the road seized her by the throat, choked her and threw her down. She was left unconscious with bruises on her neck and throat but was otherwise uninjured. Her younger son, Frank Watts, heard her screams, ran from the barnyard with a rifle, and fired two shots as the man fled into a cornfield; the Journal said neither shot had any effect. The first wire report, dated July 27, said instead that threshers on the farm chased "an unknown negro" several miles, fired a number of shots, and believed him badly wounded because blood was left on his trail. That report added that farmers were arming to resume the chase at dawn and that "a lynching is expected."

By July 28, dispatches described several hundred armed men of Harrison township surrounding a cornfield tract called the Prairie, put at 1,000 or 2,000 acres. A dispatch printed in the San Antonio Daily Light said the mob was headed by George Watts and declared, "He will be hanged." Bloodhounds from the Fort Wayne police department arrived that afternoon, and men were stationed along the railroads and highways. A later wire said Sheriff Richardson and about 100 armed citizens of Washington township followed the dogs eight miles to Boone, a Pan Handle railway station, where a revolver believed to be the fugitive's was found. The Louisville Courier-Journal put the trail at five miles and said the posse, deciding the man had boarded a train, went home late that night "still with threats."
No report named the man or recorded his arrest or prosecution.

The story moved on the wires from July 27 under headlines such as "Left Blood on His Trail" (Birmingham Age-Herald), "Lynching Imminent" (Alexandria Gazette) and "A Lynching Is in Sight" (San Antonio Daily Light). Most reports called the fugitive "the negro" and treated a lynching as the expected result; two called him "the brute." The New-York Tribune, by contrast, called him only "an unknown man," and the Indianapolis Journal reported Mrs. Watts's uncertain description of his race. An Associated Press dispatch of July 28 called the searchers "the posse intent on lynching," wording that Southern papers were still reprinting on August 5.

The Baltimore Sun, in a comment reprinted in the Savannah Morning News on July 31, recalled that Northern papers had called Southern lynch mobs a "mob of fiends howling for human blood" and asked whether an Indiana mob had so soon acquired standing as a "posse." On August 7 the Brunswick Daily News of Georgia reprinted the same comment, calling it "very timely and pertinent remarks" on the "Indiana mob." The only Black-press report found, in the Baltimore Afro-American of August 1, merged the two wire stories without comment but headed them "'Posse' After the Negro," setting the word in quotation marks.

Besides whether he was wounded, the accounts differ on who led the pursuit (George Watts or Sheriff Richardson), its size (several hundred or about 100), the township (Harrison or Washington) and the distance the dogs ran (five or eight miles). The wires identified the man as Black, but the Indianapolis Journal, the most detailed local report, said Mrs. Watts's description fit either a light-colored Black man or a dark-complexioned white man.

reader.title: Logansport manhunt
bases: An armed crowd of farmers, described as 'intent on lynching' and expected to hang the man if caught, hunted an accused man with guns and bloodhounds; he was not caught, so this is an attempted lynching (A1, A5, A12, A10).

A group of hundreds pursued the man to lynch him in retaliation for an alleged assault on a white woman (A4, A5, A12), but the reports say he escaped, apparently by train, and no killing was reported (A10, A11).

Separate Associated Press wires, an Indianapolis Journal special and a Courier-Journal special agree on the attack on Mrs. Watts, the armed pursuit with lynching intent and the man's escape (A1, A9, A10, A12), though they differ on details.
